The wind off Cape Wrath did not blow; it screamed. For thirty years, Arthur had lived in its teeth, his world bounded by the spiral staircase of the lighthouse and the jagged black cliffs below. He was a man carved from the same granite as his tower—silent, weathered, and solitary. But this morning, the storm had finally broken, leaving behind a bruised purple sky and a sea that growled in its sleep.

Arthur stepped out onto the gallery deck, the cold salt air stinging his lungs. Below, the tide was retreating, leaving behind a chaotic fringe of kelp, driftwood, and the detritus of the Atlantic. It was his routine to walk the shoreline after a gale, checking for damage to the landing stage and clearing any hazardous debris.

He clambered down the slippery stone steps, his heavy boots finding purchase on the wet rock. Amidst a tangle of bladderwrack, something caught the pale morning light. It was a flash of deep, emerald green.

Arthur knelt, his joints protesting. Wedged tightly in a crevice of basalt was a thick glass bottle. It was heavy, encrusted with barnacles and salt-white residue, its neck sealed with a thick dollop of dark, weathered wax. Inside, a rolled cylinder of paper rested like a dry leaf.

He pried it loose. The glass was cold, pitted by years of tumbling against sand and stone. He cradled it against his woolen coat as if it were fragile glass, though it had survived forces that could crush a steel-hulled ship.

Back in the warmth of the keeper’s cottage, with the kettle whistling on the stove, Arthur set to work. He used his pocketknife to scrape away the brittle wax, the scent of old pine resin filling the small room. With a gentle twist, the cork popped, releasing a puff of air that smelled of damp earth and ancient dust—air trapped from another time.

Using a pair of long tweezers, he carefully coaxed the parchment out. It was stiff, yellowed, and dry as autumn grass. He unrolled it flat on the wooden table, weighting the corners with his brass compass and a smooth sea stone.

The handwriting was elegant, written in faded iron gall ink that had turned a rusty brown.

*“To whoever pulls this from the deep,”* it began.

*“I write this from the deck of the 'Caledonia', three days out of Glasgow, bound for the Americas. The year is 1892. The night is dark, but to the east, we can still see the steady, pulsing eye of the Cape Wrath light. It is a lonely spark in a vast blackness, yet it makes the dark feel less absolute. I am afraid of what lies ahead in the new world, but looking at that light, I feel a strange peace. If you find this, know that your light guided a frightened soul through the dark. Do not let it go out.”*

It was signed simply, *“Margaret.”*

Arthur stared at the faded script. 1892. The lighthouse had been built in 1828; his grandfather had been a keeper here, and then his father. In 1892, it would have been his grandfather, Thomas, trimming the wicks and carrying the heavy cans of paraffin up the stairs. 

A profound shiver ran down Arthur’s spine. For decades, he had viewed his work as a mechanical duty—an endless cycle of cleaning brass, polishing lenses, and watching the horizon. He had often felt like a ghost, forgotten by the world he watched over. But this scrap of paper, preserved by a miracle of glass and wax, was proof of the invisible threads that bound him to the rest of humanity. The light was not just a warning; it was a promise.

He looked out the window. The sun was beginning to break through the clouds, casting a golden path across the water. Arthur carefully rolled the parchment back up and slid it into the green bottle. He did not seal it. Instead, he placed it on the mantelpiece, right next to his grandfather’s old pocket watch.

That evening, as the dusk began to gather, Arthur climbed the spiral stairs with a lighter step. He kindled the great lamp, watching as the powerful beams cut through the gathering gloom, sweeping out across the dark, indifferent sea. He was alone, but he was no longer lonely.
